questions.stem: ACL 15 contains a single entry, 'access-list 15 deny host 10.1.4.66', and is applied inbound on the LAN interface. What BEST describes what happens to traffic from 10.1.4.20?

options.rationale: Correct: nothing permits it, so the hidden final deny matches.
True, but it doesn't name the rule that drops it.

options.text: Permitted, since the ACL targets one host
options.rationale: An ACL with no permit blocks everything, not just that host.

options.text: Permitted, since no entry matches it
options.rationale: Unmatched traffic hits the implicit deny.

questions.explanation: ACLs are processed top-down, first match wins, and an implicit deny follows the last entry. An ACL that only denies, with no permit, blocks all traffic.

questions.stem: Which of these entries could appear in a standard ACL?

options.rationale: Correct: a standard number with a source and wildcard.

options.text: access-list 5 deny tcp any any eq 23
options.rationale: Standard ACLs can't specify a protocol or port.
105 is an extended number, which needs a protocol.
Standard ACLs can't specify a destination.

questions.explanation: Standard ACLs filter on source IP address only and are numbered 1-99 and 1300-1999. Because they are source-only, they are placed close to the destination.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACLs filter on source only.

questions.stem: An ACL entry reads 'access-list 20 permit 10.1.8.0 0.0.1.255'. Which address range does it match?

options.rationale: Correct: the 1 in the third octet frees one bit, covering 8 and 9.
That would be wildcard 0.0.0.255.
A wildcard frees whole bits; 8 to 10 isn't a single block.
That would need 0.0.255.255 and a different base.

questions.explanation: A wildcard mask is an inverse mask: 0 means the bit must match and 1 means it is ignored. 0.0.1.255 is the inverse of 255.255.254.0 (/23), so it matches 10.1.8.0 to 10.1.9.255.

questions.stem: What BEST describes what an extended ACL can filter on that a standard ACL can't?

options.rationale: Correct: standard ACLs see only the source.
True, but vague; it doesn't name the fields.
Both types filter on the source.
ACLs don't inspect content; an NGFW or proxy does.

questions.explanation: Extended ACLs filter on source, destination, protocol, and ports (100-199, 2000-2699). Being more granular, they are placed close to the source.
questions.discriminator_tested: Extended ACLs add destination, protocol, and ports.

questions.stem: Which two capabilities does a stateful firewall add beyond a router ACL? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tracking the state of each session
options.rationale: Correct: session awareness.
Correct: replies to tracked sessions are allowed.

options.text: Filtering by source and destination port
options.rationale: Extended ACLs already do that.
Every ACL type can do that.
That is a VPN function.

questions.explanation: Firewalls enforce policy between networks and add session awareness beyond ACL filtering. ACLs are stateless filters; stateful firewalls track sessions.
questions.discriminator_tested: ACLs are stateless; stateful firewalls track sessions.

questions.stem: Which mechanism provides confidentiality for data?

options.rationale: Correct: only key holders can read the ciphertext.
A hash verifies integrity; it doesn't hide data.
A certificate binds a public key to an identity.
A wildcard mask matches addresses in an ACL.

questions.explanation: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext with an algorithm and a key. It provides confidentiality, not integrity or authentication on its own.

questions.stem: Which algorithm uses the same key to encrypt and to decrypt?

options.rationale: Correct: a symmetric cipher.
RSA is asymmetric: a public and a private key.
A hash has no decryption key at all.
A key-exchange method, not a cipher.

questions.explanation: Symmetric key encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suited to bulk data; key distribution is the challenge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Symmetric = same key encrypts and decrypts.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes DES from AES?

options.rationale: Correct: short enough to brute-force.

options.text: DES is an older algorithm than AES
options.rationale: True, but age alone isn't the problem.

options.text: DES is a hash, while AES is a cipher
options.rationale: Both are symmetric ciphers.

options.text: DES uses a public and private key pair
options.rationale: DES is symmetric.

questions.explanation: DES uses a 56-bit key and 64-bit blocks; it is obsolete and insecure. AES uses 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys and is the current standard.

questions.stem: An old VPN still encrypts with 3DES. Which replacement is BEST?

options.rationale: Correct: the current standard.
Weaker than what it replaces.
A hash can't replace a cipher.
A deprecated hash, not a cipher.

questions.explanation: 3DES applies DES three times; it is a deprecated, slow stopgap replaced by AES.

questions.stem: Which key lengths does AES support?

options.rationale: Correct.
That is DES.
Those are typical RSA key sizes.
AES keys are fixed sizes, all longer than 64 bits.

questions.explanation: AES supports 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys and is the current standard symmetric cipher.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes hashing from encryption?

options.rationale: Correct: there is no key to decrypt a digest.

options.text: A hash output is always the same length
options.rationale: True of hashes, but not the core distinction.

options.text: A hash uses a key; encryption doesn't
options.rationale: This is reversed.
Hashes verify integrity.

questions.explanation: Hashes are one-way functions producing a fixed-length digest. They verify integrity; because they aren't reversible, they aren't encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hash is one-way; not reversible, so not encryption.

questions.stem: A legacy script verifies backup files with MD5. Which change is BEST?

options.rationale: Correct: a current, collision-resistant hash.
Also deprecated.
Encryption isn't a hash, and DES is obsolete.

options.text: Run MD5 twice on each file
options.rationale: Repeating a broken hash doesn't fix it.

questions.explanation: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest and is broken by collisions, so avoid it for security use. SHA-256 or longer is preferred.
questions.discriminator_tested: MD5 is broken; avoid for security use.

questions.stem: Which two hash algorithms are acceptable for new security uses? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: SHA-2 family.
Correct: the newest SHA family.
Deprecated.
Broken by collisions.
A cipher, and a deprecated one.

questions.explanation: The SHA family includes SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. SHA-1 is deprecated; SHA-256 or longer, or SHA-3, is preferred.

questions.stem: Compared with leased lines between offices, what is the MAIN benefit of a site-to-site VPN?

options.text: Lower cost, using the internet with encryption
options.rationale: Correct: cheaper than leased lines, secured by the tunnel.

options.text: Encryption of traffic between the offices
options.rationale: Valuable, but leased lines are already private; cost is the main draw.

options.text: Faster performance than a private circuit
options.rationale: Internet paths are usually less predictable.

options.text: No need for routers at either site
options.rationale: Each site still needs a VPN-capable device.

questions.explanation: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet, for remote access or site-to-site. It is cheaper than leased lines.
questions.discriminator_tested: VPNs are cheaper than leased lines.

questions.stem: Which of these is an enterprise VPN?

options.text: A company's own IPsec tunnels over the internet
options.rationale: Correct: built and controlled by the organization.

options.text: A carrier's MPLS service between sites
options.rationale: That is provider-managed.
That is a leased circuit, not an enterprise VPN.

options.text: A public hotspot with a captive portal
options.rationale: That is guest access, not a VPN.

questions.explanation: Enterprise VPNs are built and managed by the organization (IPsec, SSL VPN) over the internet, so the security is customer-controlled.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes a provider-managed VPN?

options.text: The carrier runs it and isolates each customer's traffic
options.rationale: Correct: provider-operated, with traffic separation.

options.text: It connects a company's sites over shared infrastructure
options.rationale: True of most VPNs, so it doesn't distinguish this kind.

options.text: The company configures its own IPsec tunnels
options.rationale: That is an enterprise VPN.

options.text: It encrypts traffic with ESP by default
options.rationale: Provider VPNs aren't necessarily encrypted.

questions.explanation: A provider-managed VPN is operated by the service provider (for example, MPLS-based). The provider isolates customer traffic, which is not necessarily encrypted.
questions.discriminator_tested: Provider isolates traffic; not necessarily encrypted.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why IPsec is described as a framework rather than a single protocol?

options.rationale: Correct: several protocols work together.
True, but it's the combination of protocols that makes it a framework.

options.text: It runs on Cisco routers alone
options.rationale: IPsec is an open standard on many platforms.
IPsec protects IP; TCP and UDP still run inside.

questions.explanation: IPsec is a suite securing IP traffic with confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay. It is a framework (IKE plus AH/ESP), not a single protocol.

questions.stem: Which order matches how a Cisco IOS site-to-site IPsec tunnel comes up?

options.text: IKE phase 1, then phase 2 SAs, then data flows
options.rationale: Correct: management channel, data SAs, traffic.

options.text: Phase 2 SAs, then IKE phase 1, then data flows
options.rationale: Phase 2 is negotiated inside phase 1.

options.text: Data flows, then IKE phase 1, then phase 2
options.rationale: Traffic can't be protected before the SAs exist.

options.text: IKE phase 1 and data flow together, then phase 2
options.rationale: Data needs the phase 2 SAs first.

questions.explanation: Cisco IOS IPsec uses an IKE policy, a transform set, and a crypto map or profile. IKE phase 1 builds the secure management channel; phase 2 builds the data SAs; then protected traffic flows.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phase 1 = management channel; phase 2 = data SAs.

questions.stem: An auditor finds two sites protecting their traffic with IPsec AH alone. What is the BEST concern?

options.rationale: Correct: AH provides no confidentiality.

options.text: AH is less common than ESP
options.rationale: True, but popularity isn't the security issue.

options.text: AH is blocked by firewalls by default
options.rationale: Not the security concern, and not a universal default.
AH doesn't encrypt at all.

questions.explanation: AH (protocol 51) provides integrity and authentication; ESP (protocol 50) adds encryption. AH does not encrypt; ESP is the one that does.
